content: Adverse clinical events that were considered possibly or probably related to the drug occurred in less than 1% of patients studied. These events are categorized by body system and listed in decreasing order of frequency: Gastrointestinal: Diarrhea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, constipation, and vomiting. Neurologic: Dizziness, drowsiness, and amblyopia. Respiratory: Acute pulmonary hypersensitivity reactions (refer to WARNINGS). Allergic: Pruritus and urticaria. Dermatologic: Alopecia. Miscellaneous: Fever, chills, and malaise. Additional adverse events reported with the use of nitrofurantoin include: Gastrointestinal: Sialadenitis and pancreatitis. There have also been sporadic reports of pseudomembranous colitis associated with nitrofurantoin use. Symptoms of pseudomembranous colitis may occur during or after antimicrobial treatment (refer to WARNINGS). Neurologic: Peripheral neuropathy, which may become severe or irreversible, has been reported. Fatalities have occurred. Conditions such as renal impairment (creatinine clearance below 60 mL/min or significantly elevated serum creatinine), anemia, diabetes mellitus, electrolyte imbalance, vitamin B deficiency, and debilitating diseases may increase the risk of peripheral neuropathy (refer to WARNINGS). Asthenia, vertigo, and nystagmus have also been reported. Rarely, benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), confusion, depression, optic neuritis, and psychotic reactions have been observed. Bulging fontanels, indicative of benign intracranial hypertension in infants, have been reported rarely. Respiratory: Chronic, subacute, or acute pulmonary hypersensitivity reactions may occur with nitrofurantoin use. Chronic pulmonary reactions typically occur in patients receiving continuous treatment for six months or longer. Symptoms such as malaise, exertional dyspnea, cough, and altered pulmonary function may develop insidiously. Radiologic and histologic findings often reveal diffuse interstitial pneumonitis or fibrosis, or both. Fever is rarely prominent. The severity and resolution of chronic pulmonary reactions appear to correlate with the duration of therapy after the first clinical signs appear. Pulmonary function may remain permanently impaired even after discontinuation of therapy, particularly if chronic pulmonary reactions are not recognized early. Subacute pulmonary reactions are less frequently associated with fever and eosinophilia compared to the acute form. Recovery after cessation of therapy may take several months. If symptoms are not identified as drug-related and nitrofurantoin therapy is not stopped, the condition may worsen. Acute pulmonary reactions are commonly characterized by fever, chills, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltration with consolidation or pleural effusion on X-ray, and eosinophilia. These reactions usually occur within the first week of treatment and are reversible upon discontinuation of therapy, often resolving dramatically (refer to WARNINGS). Non-specific ST/T wave changes and bundle branch block have been reported in association with pulmonary reactions. Cyanosis has been reported rarely. Hepatic: Hepatic reactions, including hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, chronic active hepatitis, and hepatic necrosis, occur rarely (refer to WARNINGS). Allergic: A lupus-like syndrome associated with pulmonary reaction to nitrofurantoin has been reported. Other allergic reactions include angioedema; maculopapular, erythematous, or eczematous eruptions; anaphylaxis; arthralgia; myalgia; drug fever; chills; and vasculitis (sometimes associated with pulmonary reactions). Hypersensitivity reactions are the most frequently reported adverse events in worldwide postmarketing experience with nitrofurantoin formulations. Dermatologic: Exfoliative dermatitis and erythema multiforme (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome) have been reported rarely. Hematologic: Cyanosis secondary to methemoglobinemia has been reported rarely. Superinfections with organisms such as Pseudomonas species or Candida species may occur. In clinical trials of Macrobid, the most frequent laboratory adverse events (1-5%), regardless of drug relationship, included eosinophilia, increased AST (SGOT), increased ALT (SGPT), decreased hemoglobin, and increased serum phosphorus. Additional laboratory adverse events reported with nitrofurantoin use include glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency anemia (refer to WARNINGS), agranulocytosis, leukopenia, granulocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and megaloblastic anemia. In most cases, these hematologic abnormalities resolved after discontinuation of therapy. Aplastic anemia has been reported rarely.
